clinicalPearls: Cardiotoxicity dominates acute overdose, with hypotension, QRS and QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias that can progress rapidly to cardiac arrest
The combination of hypotension, widened QRS, prolonged QT and central nervous system depression after ingestion is highly suggestive
Even a small number of tablets can be lethal in a child owing to the drug's potency and volume of distribution
Severe hypokalaemia is common and results from intracellular potassium shift rather than true depletion, so cautious replacement is needed to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia
Onset can be rapid, so early cardiac monitoring, airway assessment and intravenous access are priorities
Management principles include early mechanical ventilation, high-dose diazepam and vasopressor support as described for severe poisoning, guided by the poisons centre
Sodium bicarbonate may be used for QRS widening reflecting sodium-channel blockade
Visual disturbance, deafness and gastrointestinal upset are additional features, and chronic use is associated with retinopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are aminoquinolines with membrane-stabilising, quinidine-like activity. They block cardiac sodium channels, slowing depolarisation and widening the QRS complex, and block potassium channels, prolonging repolarisation and the QT interval, together predisposing to ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Negative inotropy and vasodilatation produce hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. The drugs also drive potassium into cells, causing hypokalaemia whose severity broadly parallels the ingested dose. Central nervous system depression and seizures may occur, and the very large volume of distribution limits the usefulness of extracorporeal removal.
additionalDifferentials: Other sodium-channel-blocking drug overdose (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants, class I antiarrhythmics)
Other causes of shock with wide-complex tachycardia
Electrolyte-driven QT prolongation from another cause
additionalInvestigations: Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac monitoring for QRS and QT changes and arrhythmia
Serum potassium with serial monitoring given shift-related hypokalaemia
Renal and liver function and other electrolytes including magnesium
Blood glucose, as hypoglycaemia may occur
Paracetamol and salicylate levels in intentional overdose
redFlags: Widening QRS or marked QT prolongation
Severe hypokalaemia reflecting a large ingested dose
Rapid deterioration or reduced consciousness soon after ingestion
reference.prognosis: Severe acute overdose carries a high risk of sudden cardiovascular collapse and death, but early aggressive supportive care including ventilation, sedation and vasopressors has improved survival; milder ingestions and most chronic therapeutic toxicity have a good outcome.
pitfalls: Underestimating lethality, particularly of small ingestions in children
Aggressively correcting hypokalaemia and precipitating rebound hyperkalaemia
Delaying airway control and monitoring given the potential for rapid collapse
Assuming extracorporeal removal will help despite the large volume of distribution
Overlooking sodium-channel blockade as the mechanism of QRS widening
